source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits
finding: Undergraduates were allowed to use public chatbots in a timed hands-on exam to debug buggy analog circuits. Authors read the voluntarily shared chat logs with inductive thematic analysis. Chatbots gave sensible hardware knowledge, but had an unjustified tone of confidence on image-based claims.
numbers: Course ECEN 3314, Oklahoma State, Spring and Fall 2025 (enrollment about 60 and 40). 30-minute exam. 5 chat logs in Spring, 12 in Fall, 17 total (self-selected). 6 buggy circuits P1-P6 (e.g. floating MOSFET body, op-amp IC upside down, bad bias, flipped diode, 1x/10x probe mismatch).
quote: Almost all factual errors came after LLMs analyzed image inputs.
limits: n=17 self-selected logs, qualitative only, no control group, no accuracy rate, models differ (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT 5.1, Gemini, unknown version).
agent_relevance: Direct source for G10: stated confidence is not evidence of correct perception. The scaffold should treat any claim about the physical state that came from an image as unverified until a measurement confirms it.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits (Theme 2: zero-shot root causes)
finding: In one log, ChatGPT-4o given a photo of a common-emitter breadboard listed 4 candidate problems and the 4th (no DC biasing) was the true root cause. The student then dwelt on the wrong lead, and failed to debug within 30 minutes.
numbers: P3 (improper bias, CE amplifier). 4 hypotheses in one reply; true cause was hypothesis 4 of 4. Student failed inside the 30-minute limit.
quote: at zero-shot, the fourth hypothesis pointed to the true root cause
limits: One case. Success depended on the student testing items in order, not on the model ranking the true cause first.
agent_relevance: Supports generating a broad hypothesis list then testing by measurement (S-states with checks). Ranking by the model is not reliable, so code or checks must select.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits (Theme 3.1, 3D wiring errors)
finding: ChatGPT 5.1, after thinking for 4m 33s, made several false claims from one photo of a common-source amplifier: said the ground clip sat on the + rail and that a resistor was not tied to the drain. Both were wrong due to camera angle and a bent wire it could not see.
numbers: P4 (R1 >> R2 bias, CS amplifier). At least 2 false wiring claims in one answer; authors attribute it to inability to infer 3D relations from a single top-down image.
limits: Authors infer the cause (3D relations) rather than test it. One case shown.
agent_relevance: A long think does not fix perception errors. G11 and G10 apply: do not rely on reasoning length; ask for a second view or a measurement.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits (Theme 3.2, the 99% claim)
finding: On P6 (a working PCB; real bug was the oscilloscope probe setting) ChatGPT said the op-amp was wired to wrong pins and said it was 99% confident. Wrong: board used pins 1,2,3. After a second photo it was more convinced and made 3 more false statements about power pins.
numbers: Stated confidence: 99%. Claims about pins 5,6,7 vs actual 1,2,3 false; claim that pins 4 and 11 were unconnected false (3 false statements in the follow-up). Model also offered 'I can mark exactly where each connection should go'.
quote: But I'm 99% confident: wrong op-amp pins
limits: Single case, unknown model version. No frequency of overconfidence is measured.
agent_relevance: Exactly the overconfidence matched to G10. Evidence that confidence rose after more (also misread) evidence: do not let verbal confidence stop the search (SCHEMA 4b).

source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits (usage patterns and student skill gaps)
finding: Students used photos to carry context: 2 of 5 logs in Spring and 5 of 12 in Fall uploaded images of the circuit or exam. Some students offloaded fundamentals to the chatbot (expected output of a CS amplifier; AC or DC at the BJT output; confusion of probe 1x/10x with volts/div), and one student near the true cause drifted off it.
numbers: Image use 7 of 17 logs (about 41%). Use of LLMs rose from Spring to Fall while enrollment fell 60 to 40. Theme 3.3: students lacked fundamentals and offloaded critical thinking.
limits: Self-selected users, small n. No measured learning or time effect.
agent_relevance: Human side of the loop: our agent should ask the user for a measurement result, not assume the user's reading is right either.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant
finding: Case study of one fourth-year EE student using GPT-4o across 3 chats (software, 30 min, 11 prompts; Pi Pico plus mux hardware, 1 h, 10 prompts, unresolved; LED plus buck converter, 30 min, 7 prompts). LLM gave accurate component info and parsed terse prompts, but hardware needed many prompts and constant human correction as its model of the circuit drifted.
numbers: 1 participant. Software chat: error message fixed mostly in one prompt. Hardware chat 2 ended unresolved. LLM computed 455 ohm minimum, advised 470 ohm resistor. Self-reported confidence went up.
quote: it does start to forget things or modify things that you had already told it
limits: n=1, self-reported confidence, no control; the same authors then ran the larger log study.
agent_relevance: Context drift in long hardware chats: keep a code-held state record of the setup and re-inject it each turn (SCHEMA section 5). The human's confidence boost is not accuracy.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP: Chat-Debugging (hypothesis generation as the human pain point)
finding: Authors argue the LLM's main value is generating many root-cause hypotheses and test plans, since humans, expert or novice, generate few. Their proposed protocol: LLM summarises datasheets, drafts test plans, proposes causes from test results, the student runs real tests and corrects the LLM.
numbers: Protocol follows Katz and Anderson four steps (understand, test, locate, fix). Software problems resolved in about 1 prompt; hardware needed repeated test-and-report loops.
limits: Proposal only, not measured against unaided debugging.
agent_relevance: Matches S-states: hypothesis list, check by measurement, feed result back. Ask for more causes only after a failed test.

source: Katz and Anderson (1987) Debugging: An Analysis of Bug-Location Strategies (as cited by Hu and Ash 2026)
finding: Founding cognitive model of debugging cited by both Chat-Debugging papers: understand the system, test it, locate the error, repair. Bug-location strategies include discrepancy detection, topographic, split-half, exhaustive and trial and error.
numbers: Not read this session; figures taken from the Hu and Ash text only.
limits: Second-hand. Experiment details (programmers, LISP) not verified here.
agent_relevance: Theoretical frame for the schema's troubleshooting states; see earlier E08 documents for the primary details.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid (as cited by Hu and Ash 2026)
finding: Programmers usually write down no more than a few hypotheses; when handed a set of candidate hypotheses their debugging success rate and efficiency rose significantly.
numbers: Not read; stated in Hu and Ash's text only. No effect size recorded.
limits: Second-hand and software, not hardware.
agent_relevance: Supports getting a wide hypothesis list from the model, then selecting by test.

source: Jonassen and Hung (2006) Learning to Troubleshoot: A New Theory-Based Design Architecture (as cited by Hu and Ash 2026)
finding: Troubleshooting learning architecture with three parts: a multi-layer system model (topographic, functional, strategic, procedural), a simulator for testing hypotheses, and a case library of past experience. Experts try experience-based diagnosis first.
numbers: Not read; described in Hu and Ash's text only.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: LLM as case library plus a real instrument as simulator is the pairing Hu and Ash propose; the LLM cannot be the test.

source: Bo, Kazemitabaar, Zhuang and Anderson (2025) Who's the Leader? Novice Workflows in LLM-Assisted Debugging of ML Code
finding: Eight novices got a buggy ML script and ChatGPT. Actions split into leading the LLM vs led-by the LLM; led-by workflows are tied to over-reliance. Holdout F1 tracked a knowledge quiz, not self-reported experience.
numbers: n=8, 60-minute sessions, 3 seeded errors; everyone solved at least 1, four solved 2, two solved all 3. Correlation of F1 with quiz score r=.93, p<.001. Best possible F1 with RF about 0.32.
limits: n=8, formative, CHI workshop paper, ML not hardware.
agent_relevance: Sycophancy and passivity: when the human is led, errors pass through. The agent should ask for evidence, not agree.

source: Levin, van Kempen, Berger and Freund (2025) ChatDBG: Augmenting Debugging with LLMs
finding: Debugger-integrated LLM agent that can call debugger commands. On Python programs a bare 'why?' succeeded 57% of the time, a targeted query 67%, and one extra follow-up 85%. For C/C++ crashes 36% of fixes addressed the root cause and 55% only the proximate cause.
numbers: Python: 57% (why?), 67% (specialised query), 85% (one added dialog step). C/C++ (RQ3): 36% root cause, 55% proximate cause. 75,000+ downloads.
limits: Software, not hardware; success judged by the authors on their own suite.
agent_relevance: Tool access to real state (the debugger) with dialog beats bare chat. For hardware, the instrument is the equivalent; G2 revise from real output. 55% proximate fixes warns about patching symptoms.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench: LLM Agents on Real-World Hardware Bug Repair
finding: Repository-level benchmark of real hardware bug-fix pull requests in Verilog and Chisel. Best agent resolved 70.7%; success above 90% on small cores but below 65% on the largest SoC project. Failures fall into localization, hardware-semantic reasoning and cross-artifact coordination.
numbers: 417 tasks, 6 repos, 7 LLMs, 4 agent frameworks, 6 h and 500 iteration budget. GPT-5.4 xhigh 70.7%, Claude Opus 4.6 68.1%, Sonnet 4.6 66.7%, GLM 5.1 63.1%. Opus file-level precision 0.928.
limits: Simulation-checked RTL bugs, not physical bench debugging; resolved status uses a project test as the oracle.
agent_relevance: Execution-based verification (test fail to pass) is what makes the numbers trustworthy: G2, G3. Gap to Hu and Ash: physical hardware has no such oracle.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench (failure analysis and tool use)
finding: A common localization failure: the agent edits the file where the symptom appears, not the file that owns the bug. Claude models mostly used static analysis (Sonnet 18.6 tool calls, 714K input tokens) while GPT-5.4 used 77.7 tool calls and 4.2M input tokens per task for a similar resolved rate.
numbers: Sonnet 4.6: 18.6 tool calls, 714K tokens; GPT-5.4: 77.7 tool calls, 4.2M tokens; resolved 66.7% vs 70.7%. On XiangShan the visible symptom is often one cycle downstream from the root cause.
limits: Behavior descriptions come from the authors' trajectory sampling, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Symptom is not cause. A hypothesis operator should ask where the signal originates upstream. G12: about 6x the tokens bought about 4 points.

source: Yu et al. (2026) ChipBench: Benchmark for LLM Performance in AI-Aided Chip Design
finding: Verilog debugging was easier than generation: Claude 4.5 Opus 47.45% pass@1 on debugging vs 30.74% on generation. Giving the waveform file helped 8 models and hurt 13.
numbers: 89 debugging cases over 4 bug types (arithmetic, assignment, timing, state machine); zero-shot (told a bug exists) and one-shot (plus .vcd waveform). Pass@1, 5, 10 reported for 13 models.
quote: most current LLMs lack the capability to interpret it effectively
limits: Bugs are manually injected, not natural; headline 47.45% is for the best model; the multi-model table was not fully parsed.
agent_relevance: Raw measurement data given to a model is often not used; code should digest waveforms into features before asking.

source: Xu et al. (2025) EmbedAgent / EmbedBench: LLMs in Embedded System Development
finding: On simulated embedded circuits plus code (Wokwi), top reasoning models pass only about half the tasks even with a schematic. Retrieval and compiler feedback raised DeepSeek-R1 to 65.1%. Reasoning models overthought and ignored knowledge that chat models used.
numbers: 126 cases, 9 components, 3 platforms, 10 LLMs. DeepSeek-R1: 55.6% pass@1 with schematic, 50.0% generating its own; 65.1% after RAG plus compiler feedback. MicroPython on Pico best 73.8%; ESP-IDF best 29.4%; Arduino to ESP32 migration 21.4% to 27.8%.
limits: Design and programming of a circuit, not debugging a faulty one; simulation not bench. First-author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Verifiable feedback (compiler, simulation) gave the clearest gain, supporting G2 and G11 (overthinking).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Founding calibration study for LLMs. Large models (up to 52B) are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false when the format is right; P(True) self-evaluation improves with size and with seeing many of its own samples. P(IK) generalises only partly and calibrates poorly on new tasks. RLHF policy miscalibration can be reduced by temperature tuning.
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex HumanEval, BIG-bench. 20-shot P(True) with 5 own samples. Replacing an option with None of the above harms calibration.
limits: Pre-RLHF base models mainly; calibration is per task and format, and breaks out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Calibration is real in some formats and not in open hardware diagnosis with images. Use the model's probability over exclusive options (G5), never a free-text claim.

source: Xiong et al. (2024, ICLR) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
finding: Verbalized confidence from GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna and LLaMA 2 is overconfident, clustering in 80-100% in multiples of 5. GPT-4 average AUROC for telling right from wrong was only 62.7%. Sampling consistency helped more than asking for a number; no method won everywhere; professional-knowledge tasks were hardest.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 8 tasks, ECE above 0.377 on average for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna. AUROC rose about 22.2% from GPT-3 to GPT-4. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522. Best aggregation Pair-Rank ECE 0.028.
limits: Task sets are QA and reasoning, not diagnosis; models are of 2023.
agent_relevance: Verbal confidence is nearly useless for stopping (SCHEMA 4b). Consistency is a hint only (G4).

source: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard and Vaughan (2024) I'm Not Sure, But...: LLM Uncertainty Expression and User Reliance
finding: Pre-registered experiment: a first-person hedge (I'm not sure, but...) in a fictional LLM search tool lowered agreement and raised accuracy. Access to the AI helped when it was right and hurt when it was wrong.
numbers: N=404 after excluding 252 of 656 (38.4%) on MTurk; 4 arms (Control 104, Uncertain1st 92, UncertainGeneral 94, No-AI 114). Agree: 80.9% Control, 74.8% first-person, 58.4% No-AI. Correct: 72.8% first-person vs 63.9% Control; general hedge 67.9% not significant. AI correct: 88.5% vs 77.9% No-AI; AI wrong: 33.0% vs 64.7% No-AI.
limits: Medical yes/no trivia, crowd workers, fictional system; hedges also cut accuracy a little when AI was correct (92.2 to 89.2%).
agent_relevance: How the model words its confidence changes the user's checking. The agent could hedge in the first person where its checks are weak, to trigger the user's own measurement.

source: Bo, Wan and Anderson (2025, CHI) To Rely or Not to Rely? Interventions for Appropriate Reliance on LLMs
finding: Three reliance interventions (reliance disclaimer, uncertainty highlighting, implicit answer) cut over-reliance but generally did not improve appropriate reliance: they reduced reliance overall. People grew more confident after wrong reliance decisions.
numbers: N=400 Prolific. LSAT: participants alone right on 36.0% of items; advice right 50% of the time; best possible human-LLM team 62.1%. Numerical estimation: baseline error 45.7%; reliance 79.7% (WoA>0.01), 60.7% (>0.5), 32.7% (>0.99).
limits: Online crowd tasks, not hardware; disclaimer helped only on LSAT.
agent_relevance: Generic warnings do not fix overconfidence. Supports G10 and 4b (debiasing prompts fail).

source: Schaafstal, Schraagen and van Berlo (2000) Cognitive Task Analysis and Innovation of Training: Structured Troubleshooting (as cited by Hu and Ash 2026)
finding: Troubleshooting as four sub-tasks: formulate a problem description, generate causes, test, and evaluate. Novices lose track of where they are in the search as the problem space grows (working memory overflow).
numbers: Not read this session; stated via Hu and Ash.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: A persistent state log, held in code, fixes the working-memory problem for both human and agent.

source: Bo et al. (2025) Who's the Leader? (sycophancy design note)
finding: Authors name sycophancy as a reason ChatGPT was a poor guide for novices: it answers agreeably even to uninformed questions, and novices struggle to say what they need.
numbers: 8 participants, mostly CS students. Proposals: LLM-side (counter sycophancy) and user-side (example prompts).
limits: No measurement of sycophancy rate here.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model confirm a user's wrong belief about the circuit; ask for the measurement (G5, no conformity to a stated answer).

source: AMSbench (2025) A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating MLLM Capabilities in AMS Circuits
finding: About 8000 questions on schematic perception, analysis and design show eight MLLMs cannot reliably read schematics. Best model (Gemini) still needs heavy edits to its netlist; no model wrote a syntactically correct testbench except occasionally GPT-4o. Local connections are guessed fairly well, full netlists are not.
numbers: About 8000 questions, 8 models, 3 difficulty levels (perception by element count: under 9, 9 to 16, over 16 components).
limits: I read the abstract and key results text, not all tables.
agent_relevance: Vision of electronics is the weak link; a code-based netlist from the user is safer than a photo.

source: Lu, Lin et al. (2026) OmniSch: PCB Schematic Understanding Benchmark
finding: Large multimodal models show unreliable fine-grained grounding, brittle layout-to-graph parsing and inconsistent global connectivity reasoning on real PCB schematics.
numbers: 1,854 real schematics; 109.9K grounded instances; 423.4K semantic labels; 4 tasks.
limits: Only the abstract and first-page text read; schematics are clean diagrams, not photos.
agent_relevance: Same weakness as Hu and Ash saw on breadboard photos, even for drawings.

source: ElectroVizQA (2025) Digital Electronic Circuit VQA Benchmark
finding: MLLMs average about 54% on digital circuit visual questions. GPT-4o: 60.39% with image plus question, 72.36% from a textual expression only; Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 62.27% with image and 45.21% text-only. Chain-of-thought did not consistently help. Models failed at transistor image questions and gate recognition even with textual and visual hints.
numbers: 626 questions, difficulty levels 27.31/40.81/31.86% (easy/medium/hard). Two models tested on full set.
limits: Textbook-style digital logic; not fault finding.
agent_relevance: Visual input is not always better than a text description; ask the user for text netlists or readings.

source: Meng et al. (2026) VeriBugBench: Framework for Verilog RTL Debugging Benchmarks
finding: Builds 2,608 executable single-fault Verilog instances from 45 projects with 19 inverse mutation operators learned from bug-fix histories; LLM-enhanced testbenches raise fault observability a little.
numbers: 45 projects, 29,834 SLOC, median 47 instances per project. Mean fault observability 36.01% to 39.54%. Prior CIRFix has 32 expert-transplanted scenarios. Expression, access and assignment constructs are 90.31% of expression-level bug fixes.
limits: Benchmark construction paper; no LLM debugging accuracy reported in what I read.
agent_relevance: Most real bugs are small expression edits; a failing test (observable fault) is needed before a diagnosis can be scored.
